This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee meeting. It was mainly about the evidence session on the higher education new academic year allocations. David Blaney and Bethan Owen were the two leading figures in the discussion about the financial sustainability of the universities in Wales. First of all, they discussed the financial indicators for the universities here in Wales, which showed a deficit and a small deficit of 0.4 per cent of income in 2017-18, which was an improvement on the deficit the year before of 1.7 per cent, but notably, the sector in England were looking at surpluses of 3 per cent to 4 per cent in the same period. The forecasts that they had this time last year were indicating that, for 2018-19, they should have a sector that's roughly in a break-even position, but that had to be caveated with waiting for new forecasts in July, where there would have to be a reflection of the pension costs, and there had been significant changes in pension costs for the teachers' pension scheme and the universities' superannuation scheme as well, and those would be significant costs that universities had to build into their forecasts at a time when their income, certainly their fee income, was not increasing, and

The first was the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which is deeper and longer in Wales than it is elsewhere in the UK. The second was the increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. The third was the current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit.

According to Bethan Owen, there were also differences in the way that universities had secured funding for investing in their estates. For example, Cardiff University have had a bond rather than borrowing, which they drew down as they were spending. So, in the short term, the reserves of Cardiff would appear as though they had significant cash balances, but all of those were restricted for investment in the estate and, over the next two or three years, would be utilised for that. Dr David Blaney explained that the estates strategies that institutions operated were overseen by either the full governing body or relevant sub-committees in respect of every institution, so there was proper governance oversight.

According to Dr David Blaney, the government was in a managed situation, but the challenges were quite acute. There was always the possibility of structural change within the sector, and that might be one of the solutions that institutions thought about, but it was not a policy position, and it's not always a good short-term response to crisis anyway, actually. But he did not see an institution falling over in the foreseeable future.

The government was content on two fronts: one was that the governance machinery within the institutions was structured appropriately to look at that, but also that if the institutions were wanting to engage in anything other than relatively trivial borrowing, they had to get their consent as well. And what they didn't do was second-guess everything, but what they did do was make sure that the governing body, or its relevant committees, had been asking the right questions.

The institutional risk review process was fundamentally designed to make sure that institutions were grappling with their problems before they become a crisis.
